newsitem.title: GREECE: Five dead, one missing after storms hit Greece.
newsitem.headline: Five dead, one missing after storms hit Greece.

text.p: Five people were dead and another still missing after heavy storms battered Greece at the weekend, cutting power and roads and causing extensive material damage.

Towns and villages were choked with masses of muddy rubble after the waters receded on Monday. Damage was assessed in the millions of dollars with thousands of homes, shops and buildings suffering heavy flood damage.
"Because of serious damage to bridges, many villages have been cut off," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas said. "This unprecedented phenomenon went beyond our worst expectations."
The national railway cancelled most services while lines were checked. Many main roads around Greece were still under water.
Heavy damage was reported around the Peloponnese peninsula, western areas near Larissa and suburbs of Athens.

Worse hit was Corinth, 85 kms (50 miles) west of Athens, where a river burst its banks and flooded the whole town. Water which reached window sills churned through central Corinth on Sunday, sweeping away scores of cars.
Bulldozers cleared away walls of debris and mud on Monday in Corinth and other towns after the water receded. Electricity and telephones were cut in many areas and were still out on Monday.
There were traffic snarls around Athens. Motorists inched to work with traffic lights knocked out by the storms.
Both Athens's fashionable northern suburb of Kifissia and the seaside suburb of Glyfada were awash on Sunday. Water lapped the windows of boutiques and shops.
By Monday most of the water had receded and crews were out trying to clean up the mess, aggravated by a weeklong rubbish collectors' strike.
Streams of garbage swept through the streets of Kifissia and other areas of Athens, piling up along pavements, blocking storm drains and choking sewers.
The rubbish collectors suspended the strike on Monday until February 20, saying it was a goodwill gesture to Athenians in view of health hazards posed by the situation in the streets.
Mayor Dimitris Avramopoulos said the capital had suffered considerable damage but its main problem was the rubbish strike.
He told a radio interviewer there were now 8,000 tonnes of rubbish in Athens and the rain had thwarted plans to spray refuse with disinfectant.
